extraction.research_question: Does using directed, weighted influence edges (capturing asymmetry and tie strength) make social-search paths from source to target more effective than the hop-count shortest path given by Dijkstra? (Sec. 1, p.1-2; Abstract)
extraction.theory: Influence of X on Y is the proportion of X's investment (interaction effort, time or count) directed at Y, normalized over all of X's investments; influence is asymmetric and lies between 0 and 1 (Sec. 3.1-3.3, p.3-4, citing Hangal et al. 2010 [5]). Tie strength from Granovetter's weak-ties argument motivates the weighting (Sec. 1.1, p.2). Global social search is treated as routing along the most influential path (Sec. 3, p.3).
extraction.data: Two datasets. (1) DBLP subset: about 38,942 unique author names and 16 data-mining conferences, January 2001 to February 2010; nodes are authors; undirected co-authorship edges weighted by co-authored papers (Sec. 5.1, p.6). (2) Twitter: 15 days of crawled tweets, about 23,491 unique users and 32,132 directed retweet edges; undated (Sec. 5.2, p.6). Experimental unit: 500 randomly selected source-destination pairs per dataset (Sec. 5.1, p.6). The Table 1 caption says "500 total nodes in the network", which conflicts with the stated network sizes; this is read here as the pair count, since the Table 1 counts sum to 500 per dataset.
extraction.method: Descriptive comparison of two path algorithms on the same source-destination pairs. Baseline: Dijkstra shortest path, measured by hop count, ties broken at random (Sec. 4, p.5; Sec. 5.1). Comparator: influence-based strongest path (Algorithm 1, from [5]), which enumerates candidate paths, multiplies edge influences along each path, and returns the path minimizing log(1/D) + log(1/product of influences) with D = 0.95 (p.5). Edge influence: DBLP = Papers(vi,vj)/sum_k Papers(vj,vk) (Eq. 2, p.6); Twitter = Retweets(Y,X)/sum_Z Retweets(Y,Z) (Eq. 3, p.6); general form Eq. 1 (p.4). Outcome measures: path length in hops and mean influence. No significance tests.
extraction.identification: None. No causal design, no randomized or quasi-experimental variation. The two algorithms are compared descriptively on the same sampled pairs.
extraction.scope: Population: DBLP authors in 16 selected data-mining conferences (2001-2010) and Twitter users in a 15-day undated window. Institutions: none studied. Era: 2001-2010 DBLP data; Twitter window undated. Generalization is claimed to "social networks" and "online social networks" (Abstract; Sec. 6) from two datasets only.

summary_md:
Ahmad, Ahmad and Vijay compare two ways of finding a social-search path between a source and a target. The first is plain Dijkstra, measured in hops. The second is the "strongest path" of Hangal et al. (2010). In that method, each directed edge carries an influence weight: the share of one node's total interaction investment that goes to the other node. The method then picks the path that minimises log(1/D) plus the log of 1 over the product of edge influences, with D = 0.95. The test uses 500 random source-target pairs in each of two networks: a DBLP co-authorship subset (2001-2010, about 38.9k authors) and a 15-day Twitter retweet graph (about 23.5k users, 32k directed edges). The strongest path was longer than the shortest in 64.6% of Twitter pairs and 45.0% of DBLP pairs. Mean lengths were 6.8 vs 4.9 hops on Twitter and 4.7 vs 3.3 on DBLP. The paper calls the weighted search "better", but it reports no measure of path quality, no outcome and no significance test. What it actually shows is only that the weighted route differs from the hop route and is longer. It is a method note, not evidence about legislatures.

For Paul's systems, it matters in three places:
- **Staffer closeness router.** Its hop cost, -ln(0.8 x strength), has the same form as Hangal's per-hop log(1/D) + log(1/influence), with D = 0.8 instead of 0.95. So this paper is a method source for that router, but it gives no validation of it.
- **Social interaction layer.** Its edge probability (events divided by the author's posting volume) is essentially the paper's Eq. 3 retweet influence. The layer then averages the two directions, which throws away the asymmetry the paper argues for.
- **Dashboard recruitment path.** The path matrix PE is directed, because receiver edge multipliers and role priors make it so. But the backward Dijkstra (distToTarget) multiplies edges in the forward direction away from the target. So the chain labelled "PROVABLY-OPTIMAL" is exactly max-product only when PE is symmetric. This is UNVERIFIED (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Algorithm 1 (from [5], Hangal et al.) enumerates all paths, multiplies edge influences along each, and returns the path minimizing Total_influence = log(1/D) + log(1/product of edge influences), with D = 0.95. As printed, log(1/D) is added once per path, not per hop, so it is a constant that cannot change which path wins. Table 2: average strongest vs shortest path length 6.8 vs 4.9 hops (Twitter) and 4.7 vs 3.3 (DBLP), over 500 random pairs per dataset. No path-quality metric is reported.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 4, p.5 (Algorithm 1); Sec. 5.3 and Table 2, p.7
bearings.system_side: Hop cost = -ln(HOP_FACTOR x strength) + w x uncertainty_cost, with HOP_FACTOR = 0.8, i.e. ln(1/0.8) + ln(1/strength) per hop. The ln(1/strength) sum matches the paper's log(1/product) term. The per-hop ln(1/0.8) is a hop-length penalty with no counterpart in Algorithm 1 as printed, where log(1/D) is a per-path constant. Solved by bidirectional Dijkstra with heuristic 0, not by enumerating paths. Edges are undirected.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Only the log-inverse-product part of the objective carries over. The router's per-hop decay is its own design (possibly closer to Hangal's original paper, not checked here), not something Ahmad et al. print. The paper does not validate the objective: it never measures whether strongest paths succeed more often. Its influence is directed and normalized by investment; staffer strength is symmetric exposure. Route cost is a heuristic model output, not an introduction probability (D-025).
bearings.verifier_note: Paper text checked: D = 0.95, the Total_influence formula and the Table 2 numbers all match. But Algorithm 1 computes log(1/D) once per path, so calling the router's per-hop ln(1/0.8) 'the same per-hop decay' form is wrong for this paper. Code confirmed: lines 115-116 (_hop_cost), closeness_math.py:20 (HOP_FACTOR = .8), and the docstring at 3-21 (undirected edges, bidirectional Dijkstra, heuristic 0).

bearings.paper_claim: Influence is asymmetric: if Y is highly influenced by X, the reverse is not guaranteed, even for undirected interactions such as co-authorship (Sec. 3.2; Sec. 1.1). Asymmetry 'has to be considered' in social search; the paper does not say in so many words that edges must be directed. Average node influence is 0.67 (Twitter) and 0.60 (DBLP), and most node influence values lie below one (Sec. 5.3, Table 2).
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 1.1, p.2; Sec. 3.2, p.3; Sec. 5.3 and Table 2, p.6-7
bearings.system_side: ADJ is symmetric, but PEBASE[u][v] multiplies by the receiver's EMU[v], and configureIssueNetwork scales PE[u][v] by source_shock(u)/target_resistance(v), so PE is directed. distToTarget(t) relaxes d[v] = d[u] x PE[u][v] outward from t, so dT[v] is the best product along t -> ... -> v in the forward edge direction. tracePath scores sponsor -> target moves with PE[cur][v] x dT[v]. When PE is asymmetric, the chain the comment calls 'PROVABLY-OPTIMAL' is therefore not guaranteed to be the max-product sponsor-to-target chain. tracePath also skips 'dropped' nodes that distToTarget does not exclude, which is a second way the trace can depart from the optimum. UNVERIFIED single-path reading (DE-062).
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's asymmetry point is enough to say edge direction matters for path search. The defect comes from reading the code, not from the paper. Its size depends on how far EMU (0.80-1.20) and the role priors push PE[u][v] away from PE[v][u], and on whether dropped nodes lie on the best chain. It may be small. A second path should confirm it (DE-062), for example by comparing Dijkstra on -log of the transposed PE with the traced chain.
bearings.verifier_note: The asymmetry statement is in Sec. 3.2 (and 1.1), not Sec. 3.3, and the paper does not say edges 'must be directed'. Wording corrected. 0.67/0.60 and 'below one' confirmed. Code confirmed at the cited lines: 547 symmetric ADJ, 586 EMU[v] in PEBASE, 594-597 source/target role priors, 734 forward-direction relaxation from the target, 740 tracePath with the dropped-node skip. The asymmetry argument holds on reading. Added the dropped-node caveat.

bearings.paper_claim: Twitter influence(X,Y) = Retweets(Y,X) / sum_Z Retweets(Y,Z): the share of Y's retweets that go to X. This is a directed weight normalized by the retweeter's total retweet volume (Eq. 3). The paper's reason for directed weights is that influence is asymmetric (Sec. 3.2).
bearings.system_side: p(a->b) = weighted events(a->b) / max(25, posts(a)), capped at 0.25 per direction. Events are reposts (1.0) and mentions (0.4); posts(a) counts all of a's Quorum posts, not only reposts, and excludes Bluesky. This is a per-author volume normalization like Eq. 3, but the denominator is total posts rather than total retweets. The pair weight is then the mean of the two directions, and only a 'symmetric' edge list is written, so direction is discarded.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's evidence is descriptive: a 15-day undated Twitter crawl in which strongest paths are longer, with no outcome. It does not show that directed retweet edges predict anything legislative. At most it gives weak support for keeping a directed variant of this layer alongside the symmetric one before path or recruitment use. Per-edge volume normalization was measured and REJECTED in this project's SNA tests: do not read this as support for wider volume normalization.
bearings.verifier_note: The form of Eq. 3 is confirmed. 'The same per-author volume normalization as Eq. 3' was overstated: the layer divides by all posts (floor 25) and mixes in 0.4-weighted mentions, while Eq. 3 divides by total retweets. The cap applies per direction before averaging (line 56). Mean of directions (line 61) and symmetric-only output (67-69) confirmed. Asymmetry is Sec. 3.2, not 3.3.

bearings.paper_claim: Hop-count shortest paths ignore tie strength and asymmetry (Abstract). Tie strength matters for social search (Granovetter motivation, Sec. 1.1). The strongest path uses the product of normalized influences (Sec. 4).
bearings.paper_location: Abstract, p.1; Sec. 1.1, p.2; Sec. 4, p.5
bearings.system_side: Overlap routes minimize summed integer distances plus one balanced unit (DISTANCE_SCALE) per introduction. There are two cost forms. Shared-background mode uses ceil(1e6 x 128 / strength), with strength = sum(weight x log2(1 + shared facts)). Work-time mode uses ceil(1e6 / strength), with strength = proximity x log2(1 + overlap days / 30). Both are additive inverse strengths, not -log of a bounded weight, so neither can be read as a product of per-hop reliabilities.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Context only. The paper does not compare inverse-strength costs with log-product costs, and the overlap router is a deliberate design choice. Shared work days and shared background are heuristic tie scores, not measures of closeness, access or introduction probability (D-025). Influence language is barred on revolving-door edges.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper side holds. The code side conflated two modes. The 128-scaled cost (line 34) goes with the shared-facts strength (line 331 provenance). The log2(1 + days/30) work-time strength (line 39) goes with ceil(1e6 / strength) at line 211. The conclusion (additive inverse strengths, not log-product) holds for both.

summary_issues: The summary says the closeness router's hop cost -ln(0.8 x strength) 'has the same form as Hangal's per-hop log(1/D) + log(1/influence)'. In the paper's Algorithm 1, log(1/D) is added once per path, not per hop, so it cannot change which path wins. Only the log(1/product of influences) part is shared. The router's per-hop ln(1/0.8) is a length penalty the paper does not print.

The summary says the social layer's edge probability is 'essentially the paper's Eq. 3'. Eq. 3 divides by the retweeter's total retweets. The layer divides by the author's total Quorum posts (floor 25), adds 0.4-weighted mentions, and caps each direction at 0.25. It is a similar per-author volume normalization, not the same one.

The summary says the recruitment chain is exactly max-product 'only when PE is symmetric'. Symmetry is necessary but not sufficient: tracePath also skips 'dropped' nodes that distToTarget does not exclude. The finding stays UNVERIFIED (DE-062).

The related link to steinertthrelkeld-2018-twitter-data was removed. That item's own extraction says the book never discusses reposts, mentions, edge probabilities or normalization, so it does not cover the retweet-influence definition used here.

The related link to chen-2016-most-reliable-path claimed the same objective. Chen maximizes on-time arrival probability under stochastic travel times, not a product of edge probabilities. The link holds only through the dashboard's citation.
gaps_exposed: The recruitment path's backward Dijkstra does not transpose a directed PE. Nothing checks that the 'provably optimal' chain is optimal when receiver and role multipliers make edges asymmetric (UNVERIFIED; needs a second path).
The social interaction layer computes directed probabilities but publishes only their mean. No directed social edge reaches path search or recruitment.

No router (member recruitment, staffer closeness or staffer overlap) has an outcome log against which 'strongest' and 'shortest' routes could be compared. The paper never measured this either, so the strongest-vs-shortest question stays open in both.
flags: The paper's influence weight (an edge divided by the actor's total investment) is a volume normalization. Per-edge volume normalization was measured and REJECTED in this project's SNA tests: cite the paper as a method description only, never as grounds to extend volume normalization to the cosponsor or staffer graphs.

The paper's claims that 'it is proved' and 'better result' (Abstract; Sec. 6) rest only on path-length differences over 500 pairs, with no outcome or test. Do not quote them as validation of any router.

The Table 1 caption says '500 total nodes in the network', which conflicts with the stated network sizes; read it as 500 pairs. Any figure quoted from the paper must name the window (DBLP 2001-2010; Twitter 15 days, undated) and the denominator (500 pairs).
The dashboard-path asymmetry finding is new agent analysis and stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
Route costs and strengths are heuristic model outputs, not introduction or access probabilities (D-025).
paul_alignment: Paul's highlights centre on the asymmetric definition of influence, the comparison between Dijkstra and the strongest path, and the conclusion that weighted search beats unweighted search. He left no notes, and his positions list Ahmad only under member-recruitment-path, as the strongest-path citation. The system partly matches that reading. The staffer closeness router uses the Hangal objective form, with D = 0.8. The recruitment path uses a most-reliable (max-product) Dijkstra, which follows Chen 2016 more closely than Ahmad. Where the system departs from the asymmetry Paul highlighted: the social layer averages away direction, and the recruitment path's backward pass does not respect PE's direction. Paul's highlighted line about "better result" goes further than the evidence, since the paper measures only path length. His takeaway should be held as a method preference, not as a validated finding.

related.why: The dashboard recruitment path cites Chen et al. 2016 for its max-product ('most reliable') chain, the same objective Ahmad et al. call the strongest path. Chen's own objective is different: it maximizes on-time arrival probability under stochastic link travel times, not a product of edge probabilities.
Both treat tie strength (Granovetter) and direction as core tie properties. Paul cites Haythornthwaite for directionality, and in the staffer-closeness-routes and SNA components.

Directed single-source shortest paths with non-negative weights. An exact strongest-path search (Dijkstra on -log influence) could use this in place of Ahmad's exhaustive path enumeration. Both are cited for member-recruitment-path.
Compares Dijkstra with A*, BFS and greedy best-first on grids, which includes the Dijkstra baseline used here. Both are cited for member-recruitment-path.

backlinks.why: Strongest-path search over social tie strength corresponds to the review's trust-propagation operators and path-length decay concern.
Both turn tie strength into path cost for shortest-path search. Zeller adds a way to fit that transform empirically (used vs available paths) rather than setting it by hand.

extraction.title: Similarity-based link prediction in social networks using latent relationships between the users
extraction.document_type: Journal article, open access (CC BY 4.0), 11 pages
extraction.coverage: Full text read in chunks, from title page through the author-contributions and licence page (text file 41,391 chars, 841 lines). Metadata hint is correct; no correction needed. All 38 items in the annotation file (_annots/a6421bb84f3f.json) were read. Every item is a Highlight by Paul Goff, with no sticky notes, typed comments or note text. Highlight colours: 1 green (0.49, 0.78, 0.41) and 37 yellow (0.98, 0.80, 0.35). Several highlights overlap and their covered text is interleaved, so fragments are marked [...]. Topic check: the paper covers networks, path-based (semi-local) similarity indices and link prediction. It contains no content on lobbying, allocation, elections, persuasion or turnout, legislators, or text measurement.
extraction.research_question: Can similarity scores for link prediction that go beyond common first-order neighbours (through a latent relationship captured by the correlation of second-order neighbourhood profiles) predict missing or future links more accurately than eight established similarity baselines?
extraction.theory: No named social theory. The premise is that structural similarity between two nodes predicts link formation (pp.1-2, citing Ke-ke et al. / Shang et al., ref 18). Common neighbours are treated as an incomplete measure, and a latent relationship is defined as indirect connectivity through second-order neighbours (p.2). Hypothesis 1: if two nodes with a future link have no common neighbour but a significant latent relationship, the link can be predicted. Hypothesis 2: latent relationships separate existing from non-existing links even when pairs share the same number of common neighbours (p.4).
extraction.data: Nine static real-world networks, each treated as one snapshot with no time dimension (Table 1, p.8): KRT Zachary karate club (34 nodes, 78 edges, social); DLN dolphins (62, 159, animal); UAL US airline traffic (332, 2126, airport traffic); NSC NetScience co-authorship (379, 914); INF face-to-face contacts at an exhibition (410, 2765); EML Rovira i Virgili email (1133, 5451); YST yeast biological network (2284, 6646); HAM Hamsterster social network (2426, 16630); KHN co-authorship (3772, 12718). Unit of analysis: node pairs (existing edges and non-existing pairs). No collection period is stated. Each network's sample is the full network as published, with no sampling step described.
extraction.method: Similarity-based link prediction. For each node i, a neighbourhood vector N_i (Eq. 10, p.6) has entries d_i at the node itself, CN_iz for second-order neighbours, CN_iz + 1 for first-order neighbours, and 0 otherwise. The union set UN_ij (Eq. 11) is the set of indices where either vector is positive. The indirect similarity Corr_ij is the Pearson correlation of N_i and N_j over UN_ij (Eqs. 12-13). The DICN score is DICN_ij = (1 + CN_ij)(1 + Corr_ij) (Eq. 14, p.7). Algorithm 1 (p.6) gives the pseudo-code. Evaluation: edges are randomly split into a training set (beta = 80% by default, 50-90% swept in Exp. 2) and a test set; the process is repeated 15 times and averaged. AUC (Eq. 15, pp.7-8) is computed by comparing every test edge with every non-existing pair, counting ties as 0.5. Eight baselines were implemented in Java: CN, PA, JC, HPI, CNDP, NCC, CCPA and SHOPI.
extraction.identification: None in the causal sense. The design is out-of-sample link prediction using random edge holdout. Hypotheses 1 and 2 are tested by restricting test and non-existing pairs to subsets defined by common-neighbour status (Exp. 3 and Exp. 4, pp.9-10).

summary_md:
Zareie and Sakellariou propose DICN, a link-prediction score that multiplies a direct term (1 + common neighbours) by an indirect term (1 + the Pearson correlation of two nodes' neighbourhood vectors, which include second-order neighbours). They motivate it with two observations. First, between 3.1% (UAL) and 53.7% (YST) of existing edges join nodes that share no common neighbour. Second, at the same common-neighbour count, linked and unlinked pairs overlap heavily. They test it on nine small, static, unweighted, undirected networks, holding out 20% of edges at random over 15 repeats and scoring with AUC only. DICN has the highest AUC in 8 of 9 networks. The margins over the best baseline range from about 0.01 (INF, HAM) to about 0.055 (NSC), and DICN loses on UAL. It also wins in 5 of 9 networks on pairs with no common neighbour, and in 5 of 9 on pairs with equal common-neighbour counts, where it is clearly worst on UAL (0.568 vs 0.792). No variances or significance tests are reported. Weighted and directed graphs are left to future work.

For Melange, the paper is a candidate source of dyadic features, not evidence about influence. The sharpest use is in the ridge-logistic cosponsor forecaster. Its only pair-level network signal is the direct prior sponsor-to-member affinity count. Every other network term describes a single node (degree, eigenvector), so common-neighbour and second-order similarity between the sponsor and the candidate are missing. The press HCoI layer already uses the correlation-of-profiles idea through Malaterre, but it uses correlation alone, without the direct term. Any DICN-style score in this system is a heuristic similarity output, not closeness, access or introduction probability (D-025). It stays UNVERIFIED until it is reproduced under the forecaster's own temporal split (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: DICN = (1 + CN)(1 + Corr), where Corr is the Pearson correlation of second-order neighbourhood vectors. At beta = 80% training it has the highest mean AUC (15 random splits) in 8 of 9 networks (e.g. NSC 0.9747 vs CNDP 0.9195; KHN 0.8839 vs SHOPI 0.8509). It loses on UAL (0.9367 vs NCC 0.9416). On test pairs whose nodes share no common neighbour (Exp. 3, compared only with PA, CCPA and SHOPI), it is best in 5 of 9 networks (e.g. KRT 0.8319, NSC 0.8471).
bearings.paper_location: Eq. 14 p.7; Table 2 and Experiment 1 text p.9; Table 3 and Experiment 3 text pp.9-10
bearings.system_side: The forecaster scores (bill, member) candidates with ridge logistic regression on prior-Congress HR/S features. The only dyadic feature drawn from the cosponsor graph is the direct prior member-to-sponsor affinity count and rate. The other dyadic terms are attribute-based: same party, state and chamber, NOMINATE distances, and an optional prior committee co-service term. Prior degree and eigenvector centrality are member-level and are computed on an undirected weighted sponsor-cosponsor projection. There is no common-neighbour, Jaccard, Adamic-Adar or second-order similarity feature between sponsor and candidate.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper uses random edge holdout on nine static benchmark graphs (34-3,772 nodes) that it does not describe as weighted or directed; it lists those as future work. The forecaster is temporal (the Congress t-1 graph predicts Congress t joins) and bill-level. Its prior graph is an undirected weighted projection, and its affinity feature is ordered (member, sponsor). Paper margins over the best baseline run from about 0.007 to 0.055 AUC, with no variance reported. A sponsor-candidate CN or DICN feature on the prior-Congress graph is a cheap candidate to test against the affinity baseline. Exp. 3 concerns pairs with no common neighbour, which is a different subset from pairs with zero direct prior affinity, so it should not be read as evidence about zero-affinity pairs. Any lift is UNVERIFIED until shown on the forecaster's own temporal split (DE-062).
bearings.verifier_note: Paper numbers match the text (Table 2 lines ~515-584 and Table 3 line ~635-650 of the text file; 'eight of the nine' p.9; 'five of the nine' Exp. 3). Code: CONTINUOUS_FEATURES at 117-140 confirmed. Corrections: (1) prior_committee_coservice is also a dyadic feature, though not graph-derived, and same_party/state/NOMINATE distance are dyadic attributes. (2) The prior network is an undirected weighted projection (network_definition string in compute_prior_statistics), not a directed graph. (3) The analyst equated Exp. 3 'no common neighbour' pairs with zero-affinity pairs; these are different subsets.

bearings.system_side: HCoI builds member-member edges purely from Pearson correlation of recency-weighted 19-category press-attention profiles (threshold HCOI_CORR = 0.6, minimum weight 3.0). Placing cosponsor-isolated members (D4) by correlation alone is loosely analogous to Exp. 3 (no common neighbours), but that is still a heuristic placement, not evidence of a relationship (D-025).

summary_issues: The summary calls the nine networks 'unweighted, undirected'. The paper never states this directly; it lists directed and weighted networks as future work. Wording should say 'treated as static, with directed and weighted graphs left to future work'.

'Its only pair-level network signal is the direct prior sponsor-to-member affinity count' is slightly overstated. Affinity is the only cosponsor-graph dyadic feature, but the forecaster also has dyadic attribute features (same party, state and chamber, NOMINATE distances) and an optional prior committee co-service term. Degree and eigenvector come from an undirected weighted projection.
The margin range 'about 0.01 (INF, HAM)' is rounded. INF's actual margin is 0.007 (0.9553 vs CCPA 0.9483). The NSC figure (0.055) is correct.
Bearing text elsewhere attributes UAL's loss to hub-dominated structure. The paper gives no such reason, and the summary should not import it.

System facts cited in the bearings but absent from the cited code have been removed in verification: 77% masking sign agreement, null co-movement, null HCoI homophily, +/-0.15 valence colour thresholds, and co-appearance described as 'display only'. They remain UNVERIFIED (DE-062).
Relation to Malaterre was labelled 'same-method'. It is a shared technique (Pearson profile correlation) on different inputs, so it was downgraded to 'complements'.
gaps_exposed: The cosponsor forecaster has no sponsor-candidate structural-similarity feature (common neighbours, Jaccard, Adamic-Adar, or second-order correlation). Its only dyadic network signal is direct prior affinity, so pairs with zero prior history get only node-level and ideology terms.

No link-prediction benchmark exists in the system. The engine kernel, recruitment paths and cascades treat a missing cosponsor tie as p = 0, with no estimate of how many ties are merely unobserved. The paper finds that up to 53.7% of edges lack common neighbours in some networks.

There is no evaluation of any system tie-inference layer (HCoI correlation edges, co-appearance) as a predictor of later cosponsor ties by AUC under a temporal holdout. The paper's evaluation protocol (AUC with ties counted as 0.5, Eq. 15) is a ready template, adapted to temporal rather than random splits.
flags: D-025: any DICN or common-neighbour score added to the system is a heuristic similarity output. It must never be described as closeness, access or introduction probability.

Rejected SNA proposals: the paper argues for neither dropping regular cosponsorship edges nor per-edge volume normalization. However, DICN is defined only on unweighted graphs, so a naive port would binarize the cosponsor graph and erase the 1.0/0.5 original/regular distinction. Do not let a DICN port quietly re-introduce the rejected edge changes; compute it on the existing graph or a documented weighted extension.

Component list mismatch: Zareie & Sakellariou 2020 is listed as a citation for melange-sna.co-appearance-and-references, which concerns negative or signed ties. The paper is unsigned and gives no basis for negative-tie handling.
Paul filed the paper under 'Path-Finding Algorithums'. It is a link-prediction (similarity) paper with no path-finding content.

Evidence quality: the only metric is AUC, averaged over 15 random splits, with no variance or significance tests and static benchmark graphs. Any system use is UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
paul_alignment: Paul left no takeaway for this paper. Both bibliography entries are citation-only, and his PDF markup is 38 plain highlights with no notes. The highlights focus on the claim that common neighbours alone are insufficient, the neighbourhood-vector and correlation construction, and the no-common-neighbour experiment. The paper supports that emphasis, but the gains are modest (about 0.01-0.05 AUC) and come from small, static, unweighted benchmarks. Filing it under path-finding understates its real use: it supplies dyadic similarity features for link and cosponsor prediction. The component list also cites it for negative ties in the co-appearance and reference layers, which it does not address. Nothing in his notes is stale against the built system, because the system never adopted this method. The closest built analogue is HCoI's profile correlation, which came from Malaterre, not from this paper.

extraction.research_question: How can social network analysis (SNA) be used to study information exchange, and what does it offer information professionals (for example, librarians and information providers) for assessing and changing information routes and services?
extraction.theory: Relational or network view of social structure: structure is derived empirically from observed relationships rather than from a priori classes (Wellman; Wasserman & Faust). Strength-of-weak-ties argument (Granovetter 1973). Structural holes and brokerage (Burt 1992a). Legitimation of information through close, reciprocated ties (Coleman, Katz & Menzel 1966). Graph theory is the formal base.
extraction.data: None. The article has no sample, unit of analysis, N or observation period. Numerical content is illustrative or cited from other studies: a hypothetical health-information example; the arithmetic of n(n-1) possible ties (n=20 gives 380 links per relationship); Granovetter's job-search sample (over 80% vs under 17%); Wellman et al.'s East York egocentric findings; Haythornthwaite, Wellman & Mantei (1995) with 24 relationships reduced to six dimensions; Wegener (1991) with 11 measures reduced to three attributes.
extraction.method: Narrative review and conceptual synthesis. It sets out SNA principles (relationships, ties, content, direction, strength; egocentric vs whole networks), five network principles (cohesion, structural equivalence, prominence, range, brokerage), and measurement techniques (graph and matrix representation, density, centralization, cliques, degree, closeness, betweenness, block modelling). It then maps these onto five information concepts: needs, exposure, legitimation, routes and opportunities. No estimation is performed.
extraction.identification_strategy: Not applicable. The article makes no causal or statistical identification claim.
extraction.scope: Population: information exchange among individuals, groups, organizations and concepts. Examples include library interlibrary-loan networks, hypertext subjects, co-workers, doctors, and East York residents. Institutional setting: libraries and information services, with a practitioner orientation. Era: mid-1990s, citing WWW, e-mail and online journals as new access routes (printed p. 330).

limitations: The article has no limitations section. Its own stated constraints are the following: whole-network designs need responses from all members, and the number of possible ties grows as n(n-1), so researchers are often limited in actors or relationships (printed pp. 328-329). Incomplete-data methods exist but are cited, not applied (Stork & Richards 1992).
Strength measures are context-dependent and vary by what is studied, where and whom (printed pp. 327-328). Dichotomizing ties by a frequency threshold discards strength information (printed p. 327).
Reported ties can be asymmetric: A may report many contacts with B while B reports few (printed pp. 326-327).

No empirical test is reported for the article's claims. Examples come from other studies or are hypothetical (health-information example; n=20 arithmetic). Recommendations for librarians (e.g., reorganizing circulated documents, rearranging routes) are not evaluated (printed pp. 330-331, 334, 340).
Research relying on titles or existing routes is said to miss new developments (printed pp. 339-340). This is a normative argument, not a tested finding.
The text is a 1996 conference paper and reflects mid-1990s technologies (printed p. 330).
Source PDF text layer is OCR-garbled in places (e.g., printed pp. 325, 332, 337), so some quoted text here is unreliable.

summary_md:
Haythornthwaite's article (LISR 18:323-342; the printed header says 1998, and it began as a 1996 ALISE talk) is an expository introduction to social network analysis. It has no data, sample or identification strategy. It defines a relationship by three attributes: content, direction and strength. A tie between two actors bundles all the relationships they maintain. Strength can be kept as a value or cut at a frequency threshold, and the article warns that cutting it at a threshold throws information away. It sets out five principles (cohesion, structural equivalence, prominence, range and brokerage) and the standard measures: density, centralization, cliques, degree, closeness, betweenness and block modelling. Its Figure 3 shows why betweenness can capture brokerage that degree misses. Drawing on Coleman, Katz and Menzel (1966), it separates sources that inform from close ties that legitimate adoption. It also argues that information becomes useful only when someone forwards it.

For Paul's systems this is a vocabulary paper, not evidence. No number in it carries over. Its real use is as a checklist against the graphs as built:
- **Direction.** The R Stage 3 scrape keeps sponsor-to-cosponsor direction. The AUG workbook sorts each edge's keys and `load_network` averages the two directions, so the cascade kernel runs on an undirected graph.
- **Strength.** Edges are valued (original cosponsor 1.0, regular 0.5, scaled by 1/sqrt of the bill's cosponsor count), which fits the article's advice not to cut strength at a threshold.
- **Multiplexity.** A pair that is tied in several channels never gets a stronger tie. Media edges are admitted only for untied pairs on the CU graph, or take the larger of the two weights under the holistic config.
- **Brokerage.** Betweenness exists only inside the retired InfluenceScore. The staffer graph measures diversity across node kinds, not structural holes.

The informing-versus-legitimating split is a loose conceptual parallel to the engine's two-factor kernel: one factor for diffusion, one for pressure. All bearings below are UNVERIFIED single-path readings (DE-062).

extraction.title: A Network-Based Measure of Cosponsorship Influence on Bill Passage in the United States House of Representatives
extraction.year: 2024 (arXiv v1, June 2024; this file is v2, revised 23 Nov 2025)
extraction.venue: arXiv preprint arXiv:2406.19554v2 [cs.SI]. Metadata hint confirmed: title, authors, arXiv ID all match the PDF header.
extraction.document_type: arXiv preprint; empirical political network analysis (no peer-review status stated in text)
extraction.coverage: Read in full: _text/139df50e52fc.txt lines 1-970 (printed pp. 1-26, through the full reference list). Annotation JSON read in full: 44 markup items, all pages 2-26. Figures 1-7 are present only as captions and axis labels in the extracted text, so plotted values are not available; figure-based numbers below come from the text. The text file ends at printed p. 26; no content was skipped.
extraction.research_question: Does a legislator-influence measure built from House bill cosponsorship, where two members accrue influence when a bill they both cosponsor passes and that influence decays over time, help explain which House bills pass? Does it beat conventional centralities (eigenvector, closeness, strength) as a signal of bill passage? (Sec. 1, pp. 1-2; Sec. 4-5, pp. 5-18)
extraction.theory: Influence accrues between legislators through repeated mutual cosponsorship of bills that pass (quid pro quo / logrolling, social capital, homophily, alliance formation; pp. 3-4). Influence capital accumulates with tenure and decays when a member is inactive (p. 7). Bill-level influence is meant to capture the 'influentials' idea that a few very influential people drive opinion and decisions (p. 13, citing Weimann [49] and Watts and Dodds [51]).
extraction.data: US House of Representatives bills, 111th-115th Congresses (Jan 2009 to Jan 2019), from ProPublica bulk bill data (ref [39]). Member IDs completed from Congress Legislators, Stewart and Woon, and McCrain data (refs [40-42]). Only bills are kept; simple, concurrent and joint resolutions are excluded (p. 4). Passage means success through introduction, committee and debate stages in the House, irrespective of Senate or enactment (p. 5). Units: bill (bill-level influence scores), legislator-month (influence I[t,i]), and legislator-pair-month (C tensors). N is not reported as a total bill count or member count anywhere in the text; only percentages appear. Table 1 (p. 7): share of House-originated bills passing in the House, Congresses 111-115: 10.98%, 7.3%, 9.8%, 11.84%, 13.49%. Share enacted into law: 3.87%, 2.96%, 3.55%, 3.31%, 3.84%. Mean cosponsors per bill: 21.50, 21.44, 21.96, 20.93, 19.01 (max 419, 425, 379, 332, 381). Mean bills per cosponsor: 235.72, 205.63, 227.45, 243.53, 250.87 (max 797, 632, 666, 695, 791). Text also states at least 87.85% of House bills had cosponsors in each term (p. 4). Median House passage time 98 days, mean 148 days (p. 11). Roughly 3% of all bills in the ProPublica data were enacted (p. 5). Bills are about 70% of proposed legislation (p. 5).
extraction.method: 1) Build monthly undirected weighted cosponsorship tensors: A[t,i,j]pass counts bills introduced in month t that include i and j as sponsor/cosponsors and eventually pass the House; A[t,i,j]tot counts all such bills (p. 6). Edges are symmetric; sponsorship and cosponsorship are treated equally (pp. 5-6). 2) Exponential decay with half-life 6, 12 or 24 months (k = ln(0.5)/half-life), cumulated monthly: C[t,i,j] = sum over n<=t of e^{k(t-n)} A[n,i,j] (Eq. 1-2, pp. 7-8). 3) Party-normalized influence: P[t,i]Dems and P[t,i]Reps are the decayed pass/total ratio summed over co-party members divided by party size (Eq. 3, p. 8). I[t,i] = P_Dems + P_Reps (Eq. 4, p. 8). 4) Bill influence at introduction month t_k: mean or max of I[t_k,i] over cosponsors C_k (Eq. 5, p. 10). 5) Compare passed vs failed bills in non-overlapping 4-month windows via relative difference = (mean passed minus mean failed) / mean failed (pp. 11, 13). Comparators: eigenvector centrality of D = C_pass / C_tot on the largest connected component, eigenproblem D x = lambda x (Eq. 6-7, pp. 15-16); closeness and strength centrality on the same LCC, Appendix A (Eq. 8-9, p. 18). Analysis is descriptive: plots, means and standard errors. No regression, no controls, no formal significance test is reported.
extraction.identification: None in the causal sense. The paper makes an associational claim: bill-level influence separates passed from failed bills. No control for bill topic, committee, sponsor or party beyond the party-normalized score construction (the authors list topic and committee as future controls, p. 17). Two features of the construction bear on how the separation should be read. (a) Authors' stated choice (p. 10, lines 417-422): a bill is included in its own influence calculation, so the outcome of the bill being scored can enter its own predictor; authors argue the effect is at most one bill in a large numerator. (b) As written in Sec. 4 (p. 6, 'eventually pass (including possibly in month t)'), A[n] counts a bill as passing whenever it eventually passes, so C[t] can include passage events that happen after month t. The authors do not discuss whether this is look-ahead. This is a reader's reading of the definitions, not a claim the paper makes.
extraction.scope: Population: House-originated bills in the 111th-115th Congresses only. Institution: US House of Representatives; Senate, resolutions and enactment are excluded by design (pp. 4-5). Era: January 2009 to January 2019, which the authors tie to rising polarization after 2015 (p. 9, p. 13). Findings are aggregate; the authors explicitly decline to make claims about individual legislators (p. 17).

key_findings.finding: Passed bills have larger bill-level influence than failed bills in every 4-month period from 2009 to 2019, for both mean and max aggregation.
key_findings.numbers: Consistent separation in all 4-month windows; no per-window counts given.

key_findings.finding: Max-cosponsor influence separates passed and failed bills more than mean-cosponsor influence.
key_findings.numbers: Mean relative difference at 6-month half-life: 0.248 (max) vs 0.139 (mean).

key_findings.finding: The max-vs-mean separation holds at longer half-lives.
key_findings.numbers: 12-month half-life: 0.223 (max) vs 0.122 (mean). 24-month half-life: 0.203 (max) vs 0.109 (mean).

key_findings.finding: Half-life choice between 6 and 24 months barely changes discrimination; shorter decay gives slightly larger separation.
key_findings.numbers: Max-influence relative differences 0.248 / 0.223 / 0.203 for 6 / 12 / 24 months; standard errors 0.0139 / 0.0119 / 0.0107.

key_findings.finding: Eigenvector centrality is a much weaker indicator of passage than the influence measure.
key_findings.numbers: Mean relative difference 0.004 (mean eigenvector) and 0.002 (max eigenvector), vs 0.139 and 0.248 for influence.

key_findings.finding: Closeness and strength centrality are also weak indicators, and the authors attribute the failure to dense networks (untested).
key_findings.numbers: Closeness: 0.004 mean, 0.002 max. Strength: 0.004 mean, 0.003 max.

key_findings.finding: Legislator influence scores are small and their distribution mean does not rise over time; the authors hypothesize less collaboration in Congresses 114-115.
key_findings.numbers: Legislator scores range roughly 0 to 0.008. Distribution mean is smallest in Congresses 114 and 115.

key_findings.finding: Bill-level influence declines steeply from about 2015; the authors hypothesize this tracks rising polarization (not tested).
key_findings.numbers: No numeric decline reported in text.

key_findings.finding: Authors' interpretive conclusion: a bill is more likely to pass when one very influential member cosponsors it than when several moderately influential members do. This rests on the max-vs-mean comparison.
key_findings.numbers: Based on the 0.248 (max) vs 0.139 (mean) relative differences at 6-month half-life.

limitations: Authors state the influence notion is simplistic: all legislators are treated identically despite differing external influences and goals (p. 17, lines 650-654).
Results are aggregate only; authors decline to comment on legislator-level rankings because they have more confidence in aggregates (p. 17).
Bill topics, committee assignments and other factors that affect votes are not controlled; authors list this as future work (p. 17).
Influence is symmetric; asymmetric sponsor-to-cosponsor influence is left to future work (p. 7).
Aggregation uses 4-month non-overlapping windows; other windows and overlapping windows are not explored (p. 11).
Only House passage is studied; passage in the originating chamber is the outcome, and enacted-into-law outcomes are not analyzed (pp. 4-5).
Authors call the cosponsorship-derived influence measure 'only a proxy' for legislator influence (p. 17).
Comparison with the legislative-effectiveness score (LES) is not performed (p. 18).
Other network measures (e.g. network efficiency) and polyadic influence are not examined (p. 18).
Explanation for centralities failing (dense networks) is stated as a suspicion, not tested (p. 19).
Authors state no competing interests; funding from UC Presidential Postdoctoral Fellowship (Declarations, p. 22). Code is public at github.com/sarahsotoudeh/LegislativeInfluence (p. 1, p. 22).

summary_md:
Sotoudeh, Porter and Krishnagopal (arXiv 2406.19554v2) build a pairwise influence score from House cosponsorship covering the 111th to 115th Congresses (2009 to 2019). Each pair's share of jointly cosponsored bills that passed the House is decayed exponentially (half-lives of 6, 12 or 24 months), summed over co-party members and normalized by party size. A bill's influence is then the mean or the max of its cosponsors' scores at introduction. In every non-overlapping 4-month window, passed bills score higher than failed ones. The max-cosponsor score separates them better than the mean (relative difference 0.248 vs 0.139 at a 6-month half-life). Half-life barely matters (0.248 / 0.223 / 0.203). Eigenvector, closeness and strength centralities computed on the same pass/total matrix barely separate passed from failed bills (0.002 to 0.004). The analysis is descriptive only: no controls, no significance tests and no strata. A bill counts toward its own score, and as the formulas are written, edges can include passage that happens after the scoring month.

For Paul's system there are three points. First, the paper is cited as the source of the CU cosponsor network's edge weights, but the built weights depart from it on nearly every parameter: an additive ×3 success multiplier instead of a pass/total ratio, a per-Congress 0.8 decay (half-life of about 6 years), a 1/sqrt(C) size discount, unequal role weights and no party normalization. Second, the centrality result backs retiring direction-blind centrality from the Influence pillar. It also shows that any check of InfluenceScore against bill passage would be circular, because the edges are already weighted by passage. Third, code comments and brain notes cite the paper for claims it never tests, namely recruitment chains and influence versus cosponsor count. Paul's 6-month half-life note is also a mis-transfer: the paper's decay applies to accruing cosponsorship influence, not to stance salience.

bearings.paper_claim: Influence accrues per legislator pair as a decayed ratio C_pass / C_tot of mutually cosponsored bills that eventually pass the House. Sponsor and cosponsor are treated identically, edges are undirected, decay is monthly with half-life 6, 12 or 24 months, and scores are normalized by party size (Eq. 1-4). Passage means House passage. The authors call the result only a proxy (p. 17).
bearings.system_side: Brain cites this paper for the CU cosponsor edge weights. Code (congress_member_scraper.R lines 1776-1788 and 1923-1936; fec/network/build_holistic_base.py) builds weight = role (original 1.0, regular 0.5; holistic regular 0.2) x 3.0 if the last action matches the passage regex x 0.8 per Congress of age x 1/sqrt(C), summed per directed sponsor-to-cosponsor pair. This is a volume-weighted success boost, not a pass/total ratio, with no party normalization. Last-action caveat (build_holistic_base.py, 2026-08-17): 2,652 of 37,076 tie-contributing bills carry 39,390 of 410,411 ties (about 9.6 percent); scoring them as passed would raise unrolled tie weight about 14.9 percent.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper supports only the general idea of weighting ties by joint passage, for House bills 2009-2019 with House passage as outcome. It gives no evidence for the x3 multiplier, the 1/sqrt(C) discount, the 2:1 or 5:1 role ratio, the per-Congress decay, Senate ties or CU-topic bill universes. Read the citation as inspired by, not implements.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper claims and numbers checked against text pp. 5-9 and p. 17. R and holistic constants confirmed in code. Summary 14.9 percent figure misread the caveat (it is the rise in tie weight, not the affected share), corrected here. Summary additive wording for the x3 factor corrected here.

gaps_exposed: The system has no as-of (time-sliced) network. Success flags come from the latest action at scrape time, so any validation of network measures against passage or advancement uses outcomes from the future. The paper shares a version of this flaw: a bill is included in its own score, and edges count eventual passage.
No outcome-separation check has been run on the system's own success-weighted CU network, comparing mean or max cosponsor strength for advanced and non-advanced CU bills within the same window.

No bill-level aggregation uses the strongest cosponsor (max) rather than an additive or mean signal. The paper's main contrast is max vs mean (0.248 vs 0.139), and none of the cascade, forecaster or path engines has a bill-level max-cosponsor feature.
No party-size normalization on edge weights, and no sensitivity test of decay below one Congress. Both are central parameters in the paper.

Per-edge volume normalization was measured and REJECTED in this project (association sqrt(Out*In) left Katz ~ volume at +0.552; row-stochastic at +0.477). extraction.title: Big data-assisted social media analytics for business model for business decision making system competitive analysis
extraction.venue: Information Processing & Management, 59(1), 102762 (received 15 June 2021; available online 27 September 2021)
extraction.document_type: Journal article: conceptual decision-model framework with a descriptive case study and simulation-style illustrations (no inferential statistics)
extraction.coverage: Entire extracted text file read (lines 0 to 838 of 0970f83c9875.txt, all chunks): front matter, highlights, abstract, Sections 1 to 5, CRediT, acknowledgements, references, and ScienceDirect page chrome. Paul's markup: no markup files were listed for this PDF ("(none)"), so paul_markup is empty. The PDF figures (Figs 1 to 6) are not in the text file; figure content is known only from the captions and the surrounding prose. Metadata hint was correct.
extraction.research_question: Stated objective (Sec. 1, p. 3 of the text, "Introduction"): "the objective of this study is to check the usefulness of the development and implementation of an integrative management information system." The abstract frames it as whether a Big Data-assisted social media analytics model (BD-SMAB) can help decision-makers with marketing strategy and competitive analysis. No explicit hypotheses or formal research questions are stated.
extraction.theory: No formal social-science theory. Foundations are knowledge management (KM) and business decision-making, plus the OMG Decision Model and Notation (DMN) standard for modeling decisions (Sec. 2 and Sec. 3). The decision procedure is a sequence of stages (intelligence, design/planning, choice/production of options, implementation). Stage naming is inconsistent: Sec. 3 (around line 162) says "information stage, conceptual design, development, and implementation stage," while later text describes intelligence, planning, produce options, and implementation. Sentiment and burst-detection components draw on text-mining and time-series methods, not a behavioral theory.
extraction.data: Case study (Sec. 3.1): 882,371 tweets about five retail businesses, collected via the Twitter search API by VOZIQ, a social media analytics firm one author collaborated with. Unit: individual tweets and comments. Time period is not stated. Sec. 4 software/performance evaluation: company fan pages of FMCG firms on Facebook, six brands, with household-panel purchase data mentioned (sample size and panel size not reported). Fig. 6 refers to ten brands. Table 1: Costco product and service categories (positive comment % and mean %). Table 2: share of social media mentions for five companies (Wal-Mart 35%, Costco 24%, Home Depot 19%, Kmart 11%, Kohl's 11%). The company set is inconsistent across the text: Sec. 3.1 names Costco, eBay, Kohl's, Hardware Depot, Amazon (line 249), and later Costco, Kohls, Walmart, Kmart, Habitat Depot (line 261). N for the Sec. 4 analyses is not reported.
extraction.method: Conceptual framework plus a descriptive case study. Components: (1) DMN-style decision modeling in two layers, decision requirements diagrams and decision logic (Sec. 2 and 3); (2) sentiment and phrase classification: Affin lexicon phrase scores, ensemble machine-learning classifiers on hybrid features to label praise vs complaint, and nonnegative matrix factorization for clustering (Sec. 1, around lines 125 and 129); (3) a linear model relating market value changes to weighted phrase/search-intensity changes, ΔC(t+1)=Σ w_k Δx_k(t) (Eq. 1), with weights estimated under an L1 penalty λΣ|w_k| (Eq. 2; the text writes "argmax" but a penalized least-squares minimization is described); (4) z-score normalization of 1-day variations over trailing n-day windows (Eq. 3; n=5 and 25 mentioned, burst threshold |z|>30); (5) burst detection on term frequency, a term co-occurrence/cross-correlation graph (threshold 0.1), Louvain community detection, and an event hotness index He(t)=Σ sentiment×volume over bursting events (Eq. 5); (6) Leximancer concept mapping and VOZIQ category/sentiment dashboards for the case study (Sec. 3.1). Eq. (1) and Eq. (2) are garbled in the extraction, so exact notation should be checked against the PDF.
extraction.identification: None. There is no causal identification strategy, no train/test or holdout design, no baseline comparison, no significance testing, and no robustness checks. Claims of superiority ("highest accuracy") are not tied to any measured metric.
extraction.scope: Population and setting: social media posts (mainly Twitter, Facebook) about large US-style retail companies (named in text; country not stated explicitly), plus FMCG brands on Facebook. Motivating domains listed in the abstract and conclusion include real estate, organizations, beauty trade fairs, finance, medicine, e-commerce. These are asserted, not analyzed. Era: circa 2021 publication; data period not reported. Institution: Chinese universities (author affiliations); VOZIQ is the commercial partner.

summary_md:
Zhang et al. (2022) propose BD-SMAB, a conceptual decision-support framework for business competitive analysis built from social media. It chains together several standard pieces: DMN decision modelling; Affin-lexicon and ensemble-classifier labelling of praise versus complaint; NMF clustering; an L1-penalised linear model of market-value change on phrase-intensity change (Eqs. 1-2); z-scored one-day burst detection over trailing 5- and 25-day windows (|z|>30); a term co-occurrence graph (cross-correlation >= 0.1) partitioned with Louvain; and a hotness index He(t), the sum of sentiment times volume over bursting events. The case study covers 882,371 tweets about five retailers, collected by VOZIQ, a commercial partner one author worked with. Its outputs are descriptive only: Costco category positive shares (jewelry 91%, parking 39%) and mention shares (Wal-Mart 35%, Costco 24%; window and denominator not stated). The paper has no holdout, no baseline and no metrics. Its "highest accuracy" claim has no numbers behind it. The authors call the framework conceptual. The company list is inconsistent, the equations are garbled, and several citations are wrong (the Affin citation points to a photonics paper).

For Paul's systems this is a weak, context-level source. The closest overlaps are methodological. Louvain on a thresholded correlation graph is what press_hcoi.py already does, using Malaterre's 0.6 threshold. A volume-and-sentiment burst index is a possible time-varying trigger for the salience-shock engine, whose uncertainty and polarization terms are currently static and estimated from the stance matrix. The paper does not validate any of these components, so nothing in it can justify changing a threshold, half-life or weight. Any idea taken from it starts out UNVERIFIED.

bearings.paper_claim: Builds a term co-occurrence graph from cross-correlation of burst vectors (edge threshold 0.1) and partitions it with Louvain to find event communities; no modularity, stability or external-validity figure is reported.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 3, around Eqs. 4-5 (lines ~194-208)
bearings.system_side: HCoI builds member press-category profiles (recency-weighted), links pairs at Pearson >= 0.6 (Malaterre's threshold, env HCOI_CORR) and runs Louvain with seed 7, keeping communities of at least 3. Homophily replication at press resolution was null.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The pipeline shape is the same (correlation, threshold, Louvain), but the nodes are terms, not legislators, and the threshold (0.1 vs 0.6) is unjustified and unvalidated. That gives no grounds to retune HCOI_CORR or to read the null homophily result differently. Malaterre remains the governing source.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-sna#Press HCoI communities|Press HCoI communities]]

bearings.paper_claim: Defines a time-varying event hotness index He(t) = sum over bursting events of sentiment x volume, with bursts flagged by z-scores of one-day variation over trailing 5- and 25-day windows (|z|>30). It is proposed as a brand-value measure, and no estimates or forecast errors are reported.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 3, Eqs. 3 and 5; contributions list line ~137
bearings.system_side: Salience parameters (partisan gap z_c, policy uncertainty psi_c, backfire b) are estimated from the static stance matrix. There is no time-series trigger for when an issue becomes salient. Go-public advice is computed per issue, not per moment.
bearings.transfer_conditions: A burst detector on press and social volume per CU category could supply a dated salience-onset signal. Any such signal stays UNVERIFIED until it is tested against Noble-Turner style co-partisan shifts on a second path. The paper's 'sentiment x volume' must not be imported as an influence or importance score: it measures volume, not access or influence. It comes from consumer tweets about retailers, not congressional statements.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-influence-engine#Salience shock (Noble-Turner going public)|Salience shock (Noble-Turner going public)]]

bearings.paper_claim: Scores phrase sentiment with the general-purpose Affin lexicon plus an ensemble classifier for praise vs complaint. Accuracy is described as 'highest' with no metric, and the Affin citation points to an unrelated photonics paper.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 1, around lines 125-129; Sec. 4 lines 303, 335; reference list
bearings.system_side: Tone intensity is the LSD2015 charge (pos+neg)/words with negation handling, used as intensity only. Direction comes from the stance readers.
bearings.transfer_conditions: There is no evidence here that a general lexicon measures tone validly on congressional press releases. The open question (does LSD intensity agree with human-coded intensity?) is untouched. Rice & Zorn's case for domain dictionaries remains the relevant source.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-stance#Lexicoder LSD2015 tone intensity|Lexicoder LSD2015 tone intensity]]

gaps_exposed: No time-series burst or onset detection on press/social volume per CU category. Salience and media-blend treat attention as static or exponentially decayed (2.0-year press, 0.5-year social half-lives), so the system cannot date when an issue spiked. The paper names the gap but does not show it matters.

Social posts enter the media blend by platform-agnostic p80 scaling. The paper's claim that Facebook and Twitter indices differ (values only in Fig. 5) suggests platform effects could be checked. It is unvalidated, so this is a question, not evidence.
flags: The paper's 'highest accuracy' superiority claim has no metric, baseline or holdout. Do not cite it as validation for any sentiment or stance reader. Anything adapted from it stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

The hotness index He(t) sums sentiment x volume and is framed as a brand-value measure. Importing it as an influence, importance or closeness score would breach the wording rules (graph and volume scores are heuristic model outputs, not influence; D-025). Mention shares (Wal-Mart 35% etc.) have no stated window or denominator.

Conflict of interest: the case-study data came from VOZIQ, a commercial firm one author collaborated with, and no independence statement appears. The company list is inconsistent across sections. Several references are miscited (Affin -> photonics paper; duplicate Gheisari entries). Verify any citation before relying on it.
The paper does not argue for dropping regular cosponsorship edges or for per-edge volume normalization, so neither rejected SNA proposal is triggered.
paul_alignment: Paul has not annotated this paper, and it appears in none of his component positions. The closest is his press-pillar position: he wants press statements, news cycles and social feeds, scored by sentiment, added as determinants of pathway change (the Bacik augmentation). This paper shares that aspiration in a business setting but gives no evidence that sentiment-scored social volume predicts anything, legislative or commercial. It neither supports nor undercuts his takeaway. It is a framework sketch, and it sits in the same genre as Taherdoost & Madanchian 2023, which Paul cites only for context. His notes are not made stale by it. The system's existing stance (sentiment is not stance; volume is not influence) is stricter than anything in this paper.

related.why: Same genre: a sentiment-analysis review for competitive and business research. Both are context-only for the stance stack, and neither validates on political text.
Both threshold a correlation graph and run Louvain to find communities. Malaterre supplies the 0.6 threshold press_hcoi.py actually uses. Zhang uses 0.1 on burst vectors and gives no validation.
Hargittai shows that big data from social network sites carries sampling biases. Zhang treats 882,371 tweets as representative of consumer sentiment and never examines who posts.
Rice & Zorn argue that general sentiment lexicons misfire on specialised vocabularies. Zhang applies the general Affin lexicon to retail tweets with no domain check.
Gives the methodological grounding for Twitter collection and its limits that Zhang's Twitter-API case study omits.
